narrative:
# EOD Macro Risk Brief – 2026-08-18

**Overall risk stands at High.**

No stories shifted risk bands today. Sixteen risks remain at Elevated or above:

• **Private credit's opaque expansion** (High) – unregulated leverage in shadow finance poses contagion risk if redemptions spike.
• **Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade** (High) – BoJ policy shifts threaten unwinding of leveraged positions; potential for sharp yen volatility.
• **AI power & the grid bottleneck** (High) – data centre demand outpacing grid infrastructure; brownouts or capex shocks possible.
• **Sea lanes & undersea cables** (High) – geopolitical friction and physical disruption risk to critical trade and digital routes.
• Six risks at **Elevated** including Treasury basis trades (hidden leverage), developing-world debt stress, China price spillover, and critical minerals weaponisation.

**Watch: Private credit's opaque expansion** – largest absolute level (8) with fewest disclosure requirements; margin call cascade most systemically damaging.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the Fitch inclusive measure (counting distressed exchanges and LMEs); the most recent Fitch signal is the July 2026 monthly PCDR at 5.2% TTM per Fitch's own LinkedIn post, representing a pullback from the Q2 record of 6.0% as older high-default months roll off the TTM window. Confidence is medium because only the LinkedIn title (not full report text) is accessible; the Q2 6.0% print (fully corroborated by Bloomberg and Investment Executive on July 30 2026) is retained as the last fully verified anchor.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings LinkedIn post (August 2026) titled 'U.S. Private Credit Default Rate drops to 5.2% in July' signals the TTM Fitch PCDR fell to 5.2% for July 2026, down from the record 6.0% TTM confirmed in Fitch's Q2 2026 quarterly report published July 30 2026 (Bloomberg, Investment Executive, LSTA). The 6.0% Q2 figure itself was up from 5.7% in Q1 2026; Fitch recorded 32 default events from 20 new unique defaulters in Q2, with maturity extensions comprising more than half.

dissent.view: Fitch Q2 2026 quarterly report (fully corroborated): TTM private credit default rate 6.0% through Q2-end, a record high, up from 5.7% in Q1 2026; 32 default events from 20 new unique defaulters; more than half involved maturity extensions

With Intelligence estimate: 'true' default rate approached 5% through first nine months of 2025 when selective defaults and LMEs included; headline rate remained below 2% for several years on narrow count-based measure
Moody's: distressed restructurings accounted for roughly 65% of all 2025 private credit defaults; excluding them produces headline rates of 1.6%-4.7%
Proskauer Private Credit Default Index (count-based, narrower methodology): typically 2-3 points lower than Fitch inclusive measure

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: More than 6 named funds spanning Apollo, Ares, BlackRock HPS, Blue Owl (multiple vehicles), Cliffwater, Morgan Stanley, and Oaktree enforced quarterly repurchase caps in the same Q1 2026 window, with gating persisting into Q2 2026; combined AUM of affected funds is estimated well above $100B, satisfying the rubric threshold for WIDESPREAD (>=3 largest funds or >$100B AUM gated in the same quarter).
items.fact: In Q1-Q2 2026, >=6 of the largest private credit/BDC funds simultaneously hit or enforced quarterly repurchase caps: Blue Owl OBDC II (permanently gated, $1.6B), Blue Owl OCIC ($34B, 22%/18.8% requests capped at 5%), BlackRock HPS ($26B, 9.3% capped), Apollo Debt Solutions ($723M Q1 redemptions doubling cap), Ares flagship (11.6% capped), Morgan Stanley North Haven (10.9% capped), Oaktree Strategic Credit (6.8%/expanded to 7%), Cliffwater CCLFX ($42B, 14%/7%). Q2 2026: Apollo, Ares, BlackRock, Blackstone, Cliffwater all gated a second consecutive quarter. Combined gated AUM far exceeds $100B. Sources: CRS/Congress.gov (March 27 2026), ABF Journal (May 28 2026), AltsWire (May 17 2026), ZeroHedge/Bloomberg (July 2 2026), Perspective on Risk Substack (April 11 2026).

dissent.view: Some analysts (CAIA, PGIM, Adams Street) argue gates are functioning as contractually designed structural safeguards, not evidence of credit distress or systemic liquidity failure; Blackstone BCRED avoided a hard gate by injecting $400M of own capital.

items.label: SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)
items.rationale: One official one-year extension has already been granted (rubric = 1), and a SIFMA exemptive-relief request was pending as of May 2026 (also independently triggering rubric = 1). No second formal extension has been announced as of Aug 17 2026, so rubric level 2 is not met.
items.fact: On Feb 25, 2025, the SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year (Release 34-102487): cash from Dec 31 2025 to Dec 31 2026, repo from Jun 30 2026 to Jun 30 2027. Separately, on Apr 17 2026 the SEC published a SIFMA exemptive-relief request (inter-affiliate exemption expansion) with a public comment deadline of May 29 2026 (TBAC Charge Q2 2026, treasury.gov, dated May 2026). As of Aug 2026, the SEC reaffirmed the current deadlines with no second extension (SEC Commissioner Uyeda statement, sec.gov, ~Aug 7 2026).

dissent.view: DTCC Aug 2026 readiness survey finds industry 'well positioned' for Dec 31 2026 cash deadline with >$1.2T already clearing, suggesting operational trajectory closer to on-track; however the prior formal extension and pending exemptive relief request still satisfy rubric = 1.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The 10Y JGB yield is up far more than 25 bps on fiscal news (rubric score 1 threshold) and the funding path, while nominally specified, has not been credibly accepted by markets — qualifying as UNCLEAR. However, without a confirmed failed/tailing auction (BTC <2) or BOJ emergency operation, the evidence does not reach the DISORDERLY threshold (score 2), per the instruction not to assign the most severe level without clear evidence.
items.fact: 10-year JGB yield touched 2.93% on Aug 17 2026 — its highest since September 1996 — driven by fiscal concerns over PM Takaichi's stimulus spending plans; yield is up ~130 bps over 12 months and ~19 bps over the past month. Funding path was specified (deficit-covering bonds, no new net issuance per May 2026 supplementary budget), but markets have continuously repriced higher. No failed auction (BTC <2) or BOJ emergency operation found; Aug 4 2026 10Y auction cleared per MOF. Sources: Euronews 2026-08-17 (https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/08/17/japans-10-year-bond-yield-hits-a-30-year-high-as-growth-data-disappoints); TradingEconomics 2026-08-14; MOF auction result page 2026-08-04 (https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/jgbs/auction/calendar/eresul/eresul20260804a.htm); CNBC 2026-06-01 (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/01/japan-pm-takaichis-budget-remarks-send-red-flag-to-bond-markets.html).

dissent.view: ModelDiplomat (July 2026) argues a near-term disorderly unwind is 'unlikely' given Japan's domestic investor base, long debt-maturity profile, and FY2026 primary-balance surplus, suggesting markets are stress-testing but not breaking.

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Multiple exemptive relief requests are actively pending and unresolved (SIFMA, IIB, 15c3-3) and a legal/documentation backlog for bilateral agreements is the cited top implementation challenge — both conditions map directly to rubric Score 1 (FRICTION). No deadline extension has been granted and readiness surveys show >80% confidence among netting members, ruling out Score 2. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-08-17 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: SEC Commissioner Uyeda August 2026 update (sec.gov, ~Aug 7 2026) confirms Dec 31 2026 cash and Jun 30 2027 repo deadlines hold, but multiple exemptive relief requests remain pending (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB non-U.S. transactions, 15c3-3 omnibus margin relief with comments due Aug 31 2026); TBAC May 2026 report identifies 'largest challenge continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with bilateral agreements between participants'; DTCC/FICC readiness survey (~July 2026) shows 79% of netting members have account structures in place and 'most respondents already prepared or completing final readiness activities', but $300-400bn in daily cash activity still to migrate (source: sec.gov Uyeda Aug 2026 statement; home.treasury.gov TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf May 2026; finadium.com DTCC survey ~Jul 2026).

dissent.view: DTCC/FICC president Brian Steele states 'the industry is well positioned for the Treasury cash clearing deadline on December 31, 2026' with 79% account structures in place and $12T+ daily clearing volume — suggesting Score 0 (SMOOTH) is plausible for cash.

TBAC May 2026 warns 'challenges associated with some remaining issues could result in a clearing market not available to all participants in all regions by the SEC deadline' and CME go-live slipped Q2 to Q3 2026 — suggesting Score 2 (PROBLEMS) risk is non-trivial for repo.

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~100% YoY for Alphabet, ~66%+ for Microsoft) materially exceeds AI-attributable revenue growth (~82% Cloud for Alphabet, ~43% Azure for Microsoft), keeping the gap wide; however, AI revenue is still accelerating QoQ (Alphabet Cloud 82% vs ~63% prior quarter; Azure 43% vs 40% prior quarter), and no hyperscaler cut its AI-revenue outlook, so rubric score 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: Alphabet Q2 2026 (reported July 22, 2026): capex $44.9B, up ~100% YoY; Google Cloud revenue $24.8B, up 82% YoY, accelerating from ~63% in Q1 2026; full-year capex guidance raised to $195-$205B. Microsoft FY26 Q4 (June 30, 2026): Azure +43% YoY (accelerating); capex guided >$40B/quarter. Sources: SEC 8-K MSFT July 29 2026; Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings July 22 2026 (CNBC, Tickeron, BigGo Finance).

dissent.view: Alphabet raised full-year capex guidance to $195-205B (from $180-190B) while FCF turned negative at -$5.9B and stock sold off 7% after-hours, which some analysts frame as capex outrunning monetization in a manner approaching rubric-2 severity

Nextwavesinsight pre-Q2 analysis citing Allianz Research estimated a ~46% capex-to-revenue divergence exceeding the 2001 telecom overbuild peak of 32%, suggesting systemic widening rather than idiosyncratic gap

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: 30+ DPD is up 29 bps YoY (rising, not flat/down), placing it above the Level 0 threshold; however the +29 bps increase is far below the +100 bps trigger for Level 2, and charge-offs per CFPB data remain ~1.8-2%, contained well under the 3% cap for Level 1.
items.fact: Affirm 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans ex-Peloton was 2.8% as of March 31, 2026, up 29 bps YoY from 2.5% at March 31, 2025 (Affirm FQ3'26 SEC 8-K, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001820953/000162828026032105/affirmfq326shareholderle.htm, filed May 7, 2026). CFPB/Richmond Fed data show sector charge-off rate at ~1.83% in 2023, rising modestly since but remaining well below 3%.

dissent.view: Richmond Fed (Feb 2026) notes 'indicative evidence from consumer surveys that late payment and delinquency behavior among BNPL users has increased since 2023' but cites no hard YoY bps figure rivaling Affirm's audited filing; Klarna reports delinquency rates 'continuing to decline' per its own 2025 press release, diverging from the Affirm upward trend.

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric calls for the latest Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate as a percent; 11.71% is the most recent explicitly published Trepp office-sector figure found (March 2026), with the January 2026 all-time high of 12.34% and a July 2026 overall spike of 51 bps suggesting the rate may be drifting higher again but no updated office sub-rate is available. Confidence is medium because the July 2026 Trepp report was not broken out by sector in available sources.
items.fact: According to Trepp data cited by Colliers Knowledge Leader (April 8 2026): 'the office CMBS delinquency rate stood at 11.71% in March 2026, down from the 12.34% peak reached in January' — Trepp/Colliers, March 2026 reporting period.

dissent.view: KBRA (not Trepp) reported its own-rated CMBS office delinquency at 13.9% in January 2026, 12.8% in February 2026, and 13.2% in August 2025 — KBRA's universe differs from Trepp's broader dataset and consistently reads higher

S&P Global Ratings headline noted 'The Office Rate Surpasses 10.5%' for January 2026 overall CMBS — paywalled detail, directionally consistent but numerically below both Trepp and KBRA office readings

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: H1 2026 insured cat losses of USD 42–47bn are uniformly below the 10-year first-half average (~USD 50bn), placing YTD at roughly 84–94% of average — well under the 150% threshold for SEVERE and also below the average itself. No single event exceeded USD 10bn, ruling out the ELEVATED trigger on the single-event criterion. Rubric maps cleanly to 0 = NORMAL.
items.fact: Swiss Re Institute estimates global insured natural catastrophe losses at USD 42 billion for H1 2026, 16% below the 10-year first-half average of USD 50 billion — the lowest H1 total since 2020. Munich Re reports USD 44 billion (also below the 10-year average of ~USD 50 billion). Gallagher Re reports at least USD 46 billion, 28% below the 10-year average. No single event exceeded USD 5 billion in insured losses in H1 2026. Sources: Swiss Re Institute (swissre.com, ~2026-08-11); Munich Re (munichre.com, 2026-07-30); Gallagher Re via Risk & Insurance (~2026-07-15).

dissent.view: Aon estimates H1 2026 insured losses at 'at least $47bn', slightly above Swiss Re's $42bn and Munich Re's $44bn, but still characterises losses as below the 10-year average

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Two rubric-1 triggers are simultaneously active: named banks offloading AI/data-center debt at a discount and CoreWeave, a named GPU-backed borrower, facing a documented refinancing wall with CDS-implied 50% default odds. However, CoreWeave's Q2 2026 earnings (Aug 11) beat consensus, interest expense landed at the low end of guidance, management affirmed no hard debt maturities until 2029, and no default or distressed exchange has been confirmed, keeping the reading at 1 rather than 2.
items.fact: CoreWeave CDS priced at 855 bps (50% five-year default probability) on July 29 2026, and the company was forced to widen its $2.6B leveraged loan spread by 100-125 bps; separately, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG spent 6+ months distributing $38B of Oracle-leased data-center construction debt, with some banks selling at a discount to non-bank lenders (Financial Times, reported May 6 2026; TechTimes CDS coverage July 30 2026; CNBC Q2 earnings Aug 11 2026).

dissent.view: CoreWeave Q2 2026 earnings beat (revenue +112% YoY, $104B backlog, interest expense at low end of guidance at $640M) and new Anthropic/Meta contracts suggest near-term default risk is overstated by CDS market; equity analysts maintain average $145.76 Buy target

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: ~13 states with active non-renewal/market-retreat conditions sits in the 5-15 band triggering rubric level 1 (RISING); the absence of a confirmed top-10 full-state exit and evidence of FL stabilisation prevents escalation to level 2 (ACCELERATING).
items.fact: NAIC 'Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics' report (July 31, 2026) covering 715 carriers and 2018-2024 MCAS data: company-initiated non-renewal rates rose 96%-216% across all four US regions; approximately 13 states (CA, FL, TX, LA, CO, GA, OK, and others) are documented with active non-renewal waves or significant carrier book reductions, per NAIC + Climate Cosmos (June 2026). NAIC characterises the market as 'operationally robust but under pressure.' Florida Citizens depopulated from 1.42M to ~385K-395K policies by Jan 2026, indicating partial stabilisation. No confirmed full exit of a top-10 insurer from a major state in 2026.

dissent.view: Climate Cosmos (June 18, 2026) enumerates exactly 13 named states with insurer drop waves, which is near the upper bound of the RISING band and could tip to ACCELERATING if additional states are confirmed in the NAIC ZIP-level data call launched March 2026.
insurance.com survey (May 2026) reports only 7% of homeowners experienced non-renewal/cancellation, characterising numbers as 'very low,' implying the systemic severity may be overstated.

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: The rubric threshold for CLUSTER is >=3 failures in 6 months; at least 3 of the 4 2026 failures fall in the trailing 6-month window, each with assets well below $10bn, satisfying the count criterion mechanically. Additionally, the April 2026 FDIC enforcement action preceding Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia's May closure independently satisfies the ISOLATED threshold, but the >=3 count elevates the reading to CLUSTER=2. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (2 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: Forbes Advisor (sourcing FDIC data, updated 2026) reports 4 US bank failures year-to-date in 2026: Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust (Jan 30, $261M assets, CRE-linked per Bisnow Feb 2 2026), Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia (May 1, preceded by FDIC enforcement action April 2026), Kentland Federal Savings and Loan (Jul 10), and a fourth unnamed institution. At least 3 of these 4 fall within the trailing 6-month window (Feb 17 - Aug 17 2026). FDIC/Bisnow confirm CRE real-estate loan exposure as a contributing factor for Metropolitan Capital; the FDIC issued a pre-closure enforcement action against Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia in April 2026.

dissent.view: Bankrate (Feb 18 2026 update) reported only 1 failure in 2026 at that time (Metropolitan Capital), and did not confirm CRE as the primary regulatory cited cause; FDIC has not released a formal post-seizure analysis citing CRE concentration for any 2026 failure as of this date, leaving causal attribution partially inferential.

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The Fitch ABS index is the primary, authoritative source for securitized subprime auto 60+ DPD; June 2026 at 5.67% is the latest published monthly figure, well above historical norms but meaningfully off the January 2026 record peak of 6.90%, reflecting seasonal improvement while remaining structurally elevated.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS 60-day-plus delinquency rate in June 2026 was 5.67%, down 64 basis points year-over-year, per Wolf Street (August 13, 2026) citing Fitch Ratings directly.

dissent.view: January 2026 peak reading of 6.90% (record high, 32-year) per Fitch Ratings — still cited in some July 2026 commentary as the headline figure without updating to June
Philadelphia Fed Q3 2025 consumer-level 60+ DPD (all auto, not subprime-only) peaked at 1.68% — different universe and methodology than Fitch ABS index

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: Lecornu holds no working majority and repeatedly invoked Article 49.3-equivalent constitutional bypass mechanisms, survived multiple no-confidence votes across Oct 2025–Feb 2026, and governs through targeted concessions — a paradigmatic FRAGILE (1) situation. No evidence of a government collapse, PM resignation, or snap election call has emerged since the budget passage on 2 February 2026.
items.fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's minority government survived two no-confidence motions on 2 February 2026 — the final pair tied to the 2026 budget passage — with the LFI-led motion drawing 260 votes vs. the 289 needed, and the RN motion drawing only 135 votes; the 2026 budget was formally adopted the same day. Lecornu governs without a parliamentary majority, relying on Socialist and Les Républicains abstentions. Source: Al Jazeera, 2026-02-02 (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/2/france-adopts-2026-budget-after-two-no-confidence-votes-fail); Reuters via Yahoo, 2026-01-27 (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/french-government-survives-no-confidence-190649618.html).

dissent.view: A Yahoo/AP report (~March 2026) references Bayrou announcing a confidence vote for 8 September — but corroborating sources confirm Bayrou fell on 8 September 2025 (pre-Lecornu), making this a timeline artefact rather than a competing current reading.

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Two new IMF arrangements in the trailing 6 months maps exactly to the RISING band (1-2 new IMF arrangements); no missed coupon was found, and the count falls short of the >=3 threshold required for CLUSTER.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: ESMA's most recent formal assessment (Jun 2026) confirms improved liquidity buffers and no active margin crisis; absent any regulator flag of current LDI liquidity risk or a documented forced-selling episode in 2026, the evidence maps squarely to rubric band 0 (buffers adequate, no margin stress).

dissent.view: ESMA's end-2024 data notes 'a subset of funds might still face challenges' under extreme shocks, implying residual tail risk that has not been fully eliminated

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

items.fact: US side: House Foreign Affairs Committee passed 20 export control measures incl. MATCH Act (April 24, 2026, SCMP) targeting DUV lithography to China; Commerce Sec. Lutnick held private meetings pressing ASML on EUV compliance (June 2026, Bloomberg/Yahoo Finance); ASML China revenue share fell 36%->19% Q4-2025 to Q1-2026 confirming volume impact. items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: Licensing is case-by-case / whitelist (general licences restricted to a handful of named producers) with real-world processing times of 60-120+ days far exceeding the 30-day threshold, and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added to the control list in the trailing 3 months via the 2026 catalogue update — all three SLOWING triggers are met. No categorical denial to a country or announced licensing suspension exists that would support a FROZEN (2) rating, and market data show exports continuing at positive YoY growth, capping the escalation read at 1.
items.fact: The April 2025 MOFCOM licensing regime (Announcement No. 28/related notices) requiring non-automatic, case-by-case export licences for dysprosium, terbium, and Dy/Tb-containing NdFeB and SmCo magnets was never suspended and remains fully in force as of August 2026. Statutory review target is 45 working days (~9 weeks), but in practice heavy-REE approvals routinely run 60-120+ days; a June 2025 US-China diplomatic deal produced a MOFCOM statement to 'review and approve eligible applications in accordance with law' yet Trump's August 2026 threats of 200% tariffs signal Washington remains unsatisfied with throughput. The 2026 Import-Export Licensing Catalogue added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories. Source: blog.gettransport.com (July 7 2026), china-briefing.com, merics.org, arnold magnetics (Feb 2026), certivo.com (March 2026).

dissent.view: Duramag (Dec 2025) and Arnold Magnetics (Feb 2026) characterise approvals as 'rare, documentation-intensive and unpredictable' with applications on hold indefinitely, which could support a borderline FROZEN read for heavy-REE end-uses; however no MOFCOM-announced categorical denial or >30-day suspension of issuance is documented.

items.fact: India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty 'in abeyance' after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, physically cut flows via Baglihar Dam on the Chenab (May 2025), stopped hydrological data sharing, and Pakistan reported abrupt flow drops at Marala (Chenab: 21,887 to 5,689 cusecs) in May 2026. Pakistan's Defence Minister stated 'the moment we feel our national security is under threat...we will go to war' (June 2026 CNBC). India's Home Minister vowed the treaty 'will never be restored' (June 2025, reiterated 2026). Sources: Chatham House April 2026; CNBC June 22 2026; Dawn June 2026; Britannica July 2026.

dissent.view: GERD/Nile dispute assessed as TENSE (level 1) not CRISIS: Egypt raised GERD at UNSC and signed military port agreements with Eritrea/Djibouti (strategic posturing), but no armed clash or deliberate Nile flow cut-off has occurred; analysts (pppescp.com, March 2026) assess armed conflict likelihood as 'relatively low'.
Chatham House (April 2026) frames IWT suspension as 'temporary' and calls for re-engagement, suggesting some analysts view the situation as still short of full crisis.

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric level 2 requires the deadline to be missed without final rules; that condition is unambiguously met — the July 18, 2026 statutory deadline passed with zero finalized implementing regulations across all five responsible agencies, constituting a clear deadline miss with no court stay or compliance-failure event needed to trigger level 2.
items.fact: The statutory one-year deadline of July 18, 2026 passed without any final rules from the OCC, FDIC, NCUA, Federal Reserve, FinCEN, or OFAC; all major rule packages remained at the proposed/comment stage, with some comment periods still open as late as August 21, 2026. Sources: Crowdfund Insider (July 2026): 'Federal banking and financial regulators have allowed the statutory one-year period for completing implementing regulations under the GENIUS Act to lapse without delivering finalized rules.' CoinPaprika (July 19, 2026): 'The Treasury Department and four primary regulators left every major rule package as a proposal.' OCC Bulletin 2026-3 (Feb 25, 2026) confirmed only an NPRM was issued.

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The rubric requires the signed NBS figure exactly as published; +3.5% YoY for July 2026 is confirmed by the primary NBS release dated 2026-08-10 and corroborated by Xinhua/China Daily. The engine scores on the SIZE of the move: +3.5% is a meaningful positive reading signalling cost-push input-price pressure being exported globally, though it moderated from June's +4.1%.
items.fact: NBS press release t20260810_1965017 (released 2026-08-10): 'In July 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.5% year on year and decreased by 0.7% month on month.' Source: https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)
items.rationale: Eight distinct new measures across major economies (US, China, EU, UK) in the trailing 3 months, including a broad 12.5% Section 301 tariff across Chinese goods and explicit tit-for-tat export controls, exceeds the rubric threshold of >=4 new measures and includes a broad tariff round >=10% across a sector, mapping unambiguously to level 2 (ESCALATING). The underlying Nov 2025 truce framework remains nominally in place but is being actively eroded by new unilateral actions on both sides.
items.fact: In the trailing 3 months (mid-May to mid-Aug 2026), at least 8 distinct new measures were recorded: (1) USTR 12.5% Section 301 tariff on broad Chinese goods, effective 24 Jul 2026 (China Briefing, updated 24 Jul 2026; USTR); (2) US 15% tariffs on Chinese polysilicon + additional 12.5% Section 301 duties, announced 5 Aug 2026 (Polymarket summary); (3) China export controls on drone exports to US + ban on 6 US entities, 5 Aug 2026 (Fortune/Euronews); (4) China provisional anti-dumping deposits up to 54.3% on US/Mexican pecans, effective 11 Aug 2026 (MOFCOM/Global Times); (5) China export bans on 14 European companies, ~3 Aug 2026 (Mondaq/Steptoe); (6) EU definitive AD duty amendment on Chinese tinplate steel, 16 Apr 2026 (EU Reg. 2026/843); (7) UK definitive AD on Chinese tin mill products, 12 Mar 2026 (UK TRA); (8) US Commerce final LTFV determination on Chinese hardwood plywood, 21 Jul 2026 (Federal Register).

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials and USA Rare Earth) appear by name on MOFCOM's export control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying the rubric's definition of score 1 (entity-specific). The listing does not extend categorically to the US rare-earth sector as a class, and multiple analysts explicitly characterise it as firm-specific, precluding score 2.
items.fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to China's export control list, explicitly including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The measure bars Chinese exporters from supplying dual-use items to the named firms and prohibits any party from transferring China-origin dual-use goods to them. Multiple corroborating sources (Benchmark Minerals, SMM/Metal.com, Trivium China, StockTitan citing Reuters) confirm the listing; market reaction was muted (MP Materials roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher on the day), consistent with an entity-specific rather than sector-wide ban. The restriction is explicitly firm-specific: 'The measure is entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US' (Benchmark Minerals, 25 June 2026).

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: The index is rising both MoM (+0.6%) and YoY (+1.0%), and sits at a 3-year high (131.1), firmly placing it in the ELEVATED band; the MoM gain of 0.6% is well below the 3% threshold required for band 1's upper boundary and far below the 5% MoM or 10% 3-month thresholds needed for SPIKING (band 2). The 3-month cumulative move (Mar 128.5 → Jul 131.1) is roughly +2%, also below the 10% SPIKING trigger.
items.fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6% MoM from June's 130.3 and up 1.0% YoY. Released 7 August 2026. Source: fao.org/newsroom/detail/fao-food-price-index-edges-up-amid-weather--energy-and-geopolitical-concerns/en

items.label: Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Three or more named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, El Teniente) have confirmed, physically measured production cuts active in 2026, and multiple major financial institutions have revised global copper balances to a deficit — both prongs of the rubric\'s CLUSTER threshold (value=2) are satisfied.
items.fact: As of mid-2026, at least three top-20 copper mines carry confirmed, active production cuts: (1) Grasberg (world\'s #2 copper mine) — Freeport delayed full restart to early 2028, targeting only ~65% capacity in H2 2026 vs. pre-incident ~1.7 billion lb/yr; copper output guided at ~700 million lb in 2026, down ~59% from plan (mining.com, May 8 2026). (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC, top-5 mine) — seismic/flood damage in 2025 cut 2026 guidance to 290,000–330,000 t vs. original 420,000–600,000 t target; Q2 2026 actual output was 64,328 t (Ivanhoe Q2 release, July 8 2026). (3) Codelco El Teniente (world\'s largest underground copper mine) — fatal tunnel collapse in 2025 led general manager to state production will be depressed for the next five years (CNBC, March 10 2026). Additional disruptions: Capstone Mantoverde strike (halted Jan 2026); CMOC TFM strike (June 2026); Chilean output down 9% YoY in March 2026 (Cochilco). Multiple institutions forecast a 2026 market deficit: ICSG revised from a 209,000 t surplus to a 150,000 t deficit; J.P. Morgan 330,000 t deficit; Morgan Stanley 600,000 t; ING 600,000 t (cruxinvestor.com, May 26 2026).

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
